source_text: Ἐφ' ὅπερ δ' ἂν τὰ μέρη φέρηται, ἐπὶ τοῦτο καὶ τὸ ὅλον συνωσθή σεται δηλονότι. Εἰ δὲ λίθοι καὶ ξύλα καὶ τὰ γεηρὰ πάντα φέρεται πρὸς τὸ κάτω, αὕτη ἂν εἴη καὶ τῇ ὅλῃ γῇ οἰκεῖα καὶ προσήκουσα θέσις· κἄν τι τῶν κούφων φέρηται ἀπὸ τοῦ μέσου, δηλονότι πρὸς τὸ ἀνώτατον κινηθήσεται. Ὥστε οἰκεία φορὰ τοῖς βαρυτάτοις ἡ πρὸς τὸ κάτω· κάτω δὲ ὁ λόγος μέσον ἔδειξεν. Μὴ οὖν θαυμάσῃς εἰ μηδαμοῦ ἐκπίπτει ἡ γῆ, τὴν κατὰ φύσιν χώραν τὸ μέσον ἔχουσα. Πᾶσα γὰρ ἀνάγκη μένειν αὐτὴν κατὰ χώραν, ἢ παρὰ φύσιν κινουμένην τῆς οἰκείας ἕδρας ἐξίστασθαι. Τούτων δ' ἄν σοι δοκῇ τι πιθανὸν εἶναι τῶν εἰρημένων, ἐπὶ τὴν οὕτω ταῦτα διαταξαμένην τοῦ Θεοῦ σοφίαν μετάθες τὸ θαῦμα. Οὐ γὰρ ἐλαττοῦται ἡ ἐπὶ τοῖς μεγίστοις ἔκπληξις, ἐπειδὰν ὁ τρόπος καθ' ὃν γίνεταί τι τῶν παραδόξων ἐξευρεθῇ· εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἀλλὰ τό γε ἁπλοῦν τῆς πίστεως ἰσχυρότερον ἔστω τῶν λογικῶν ἀποδείξεων. 1.11 Τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ περὶ οὐρανοῦ εἴποιμεν, ὅτι πολυφωνότατοι πραγματεῖαι τοῖς σοφοῖς τοῦ κόσμου περὶ τῆς οὐρανίου φύσεως καταβέβληνται. Καὶ οἱ μὲν σύνθετον αὐτὸν ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων στοιχείων εἰρήκασιν, ὡς ἁπτὸν ὄντα καὶ ὁρατὸν, καὶ μετέχοντα γῆς μὲν διὰ τὴν ἀντιτυπίαν, πυρὸς δὲ, διὰ τὸ καθορᾶσθαι, τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν, διὰ τὴν μίξιν. Οἱ δὲ τοῦτον ὡς ἀπίθανον παρωσάμενοι τὸν λόγον, πέμπτην τινὰ σώματος φύσιν εἰς οὐρανοῦ σύστασιν οἴκοθεν καὶ παρ' ἑαυτῶν ἀποσχεδιάσαντες ἐπεισήγαγον. Καὶ ἔστι τι παρ' αὐτοῖς τὸ αἰθέριον σῶμα, ὃ μήτε πῦρ, φησὶ, μήτε ἀὴρ, μήτε γῆ, μήτε ὕδωρ, μήτε ὅλως ὅπερ ἓν τῶν ἁπλῶν· διότι τοῖς μὲν ἁπλοῖς οἰκεία κίνησις ἡ ἐπ' εὐθείας, τῶν μὲν κούφων ἐπὶ τὸ ἄνω φερομένων, τῶν δὲ βαρέων ἐπὶ τὸ κάτω. Οὔτε δὲ τὸ ἄνω καὶ τὸ κάτω τῇ κυκλικῇ περιδινήσει ταὐτόν· καὶ ὅλως τὴν εὐθεῖαν πρὸς τὴν ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ περιφορὰν πλείστην ἀπόστασιν ἔχειν. Ὧν δὲ αἱ κατὰ φύσιν κινήσεις παρηλλαγμέναι τυγχάνουσιν, τούτων ἀνάγκη, φασὶ, παρηλ λάχθαι καὶ τὰς οὐσίας. Ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδὲ ἐκ τῶν πρώτων σωμάτων, ἃ δὴ στοιχεῖα καλοῦμεν, σύνθετον εἶναι δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ὑποθέσθαι τὸν οὐρανὸν, τῷ τὰ ἐκ διαφόρων συγκείμενα μὴ δύνασθαι ὁμαλὴν καὶ ἀβίαστον ἔχειν τὴν κίνησιν, ἑκάστου τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων ἁπλῶν τοῖς συνθέτοις ἄλλην καὶ ἄλλην ὁρμὴν παρὰ τῆς φύσεως ἔχοντος. Διὸ πρῶτον μὲν καμάτῳ συνέχεται ἐν τῇ συνεχεῖ κινήσει τὰ σύνθετα, διὰ τὸ μίαν κίνησιν μὴ δύνασθαι πᾶσιν εὐάρμοστον εἶναι καὶ φίλην τοῖς ἐναντίοις· ἀλλὰ τὴν τῷ κούφῳ οἰκείαν, πολεμίαν εἶναι τῷ βαρυτάτῳ. Ὅταν μὲν γὰρ πρὸς τὰ ἄνω κινώμεθα, βαρυ νόμεθα τῷ γεώδει· ὅταν δὲ πρὸς τὰ κάτω φερώμεθα, βιαζόμεθα τὸ πυρῶδες, παρὰ φύσιν αὐτὸ πρὸς τὸ κάτω καθέλκοντες. Ἡ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἐναντία διολκὴ τῶν στοιχείων, διαπτώσεώς ἐστιν ἀφορμή. Τὸ γὰρ ἠναγκασμένον καὶ παρὰ φύσιν, ἐπ' ὀλίγον ἀντισχὸν, καὶ τοῦτο βιαίως καὶ μόλις, ταχὺ διελύθη εἰς τὰ ἐξ ὧν συνετέθη, ἑκάστου τῶν συνελθόν των πρὸς τὴν οἰκείαν χώραν ἐπανιόντος.
thought_title: The earth's natural place and the philosophers' theories of heaven
orientation: Basil is answering objections about why the earth stays in place, then turns to what the wise of the world have said about the nature of heaven.
pass_a_gloss: And toward whatever the parts are carried, toward this also the whole will clearly be pushed together. But if stones and wood and all earthy things are carried toward the downward, this would also be the proper and fitting position for the whole earth; and if any of the light things is carried from the middle, clearly it will be moved toward the highest. So that the proper motion for the heaviest things is the one toward the downward; and the downward, reason has shown, is the middle. Do not then wonder if the earth nowhere falls out, having the middle as its natural place. For there is every necessity that it remain in its place, or that, being moved contrary to nature, it depart from its proper seat. And if any of these things that have been said seems to you to be persuasive, transfer the wonder to the wisdom of God that ordered these things thus. For the astonishment at the greatest things is not lessened, whenever the manner in which something of the paradoxes happens is discovered; but if not, at least let the simplicity of faith be stronger than logical demonstrations. 1.11 And these same things we might also say about heaven, that very many-worded treatises have been laid down by the wise of the world about the heavenly nature. And some have said that it is composite from the four elements, as being tangible and visible, and partaking of earth because of the resistance, and of fire because of being seen, and of the remaining ones because of the mixture. But others, thrusting aside this account as unpersuasive, introduced a certain fifth nature of body for the constitution of heaven, improvising it from themselves and by themselves. And there is among them the ethereal body, which is neither fire, they say, nor air, nor earth, nor water, nor at all whatever one of the simple things; because for the simple things the proper motion is the one in a straight line, the light things being carried upward, and the heavy things downward. But neither is the upward and the downward the same as the circular whirling; and in general the straight line has the greatest distance from the circular revolution. And of those whose natural motions happen to be different, of these it is necessary, they say, that the substances also be different. But indeed neither is it possible for us to suppose the heaven to be composite from the first bodies, which indeed we call elements, because the things composed from different things cannot have smooth and unforced motion, each of the simple things existing in the composites having one and another impulse from nature. Therefore first the composite things are held together with labor in the continuous motion, because one motion cannot be well-fitted and friendly to all the contraries; but the motion proper to the light thing is hostile to the heaviest thing. For whenever we are moved toward the upward, we are weighed down by the earthy; but whenever we are carried toward the downward, we force the fiery, dragging it contrary to nature toward the downward. And the dragging of the elements toward the contraries is an occasion of falling apart. For the forced and contrary to nature, having resisted for a little, and this violently and scarcely, quickly is dissolved into the things from which it was composed, each of the things that came together returning to its proper place.

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of γεηρά as things of earth, matching Basil's contrast with light things
Renders the superlative literally to convey Basil's ironic tone about the philosophers' verbosity

choices.english: a certain fifth nature of body
choices.why: Keeps the indefinite τις and the literal 'nature of body' to preserve the philosophical terminology
Renders both expressions to preserve the redundancy emphasizing their self-invented theory
Literal rendering of the philosophical term for solidity or resistance to touch

choices.english: is an occasion of falling apart
choices.why: Keeps ἀφορμή as 'occasion' or 'starting point' rather than over-translating as 'cause'

pass_b_english: And clearly, wherever the parts are carried, the whole will be pushed together toward that same place. If stones and wood and all earthy things are carried downward, then this would also be the proper and fitting position for the whole earth. And if any light thing is carried from the middle, clearly it will move toward the highest point. So the proper movement for the heaviest things is downward, and reason has shown that downward means toward the middle. Do not be surprised, then, that the earth never falls out of place, since it holds the middle as its natural position. For it is absolutely necessary that it remain in place, or else, if it moves contrary to nature, it departs from its proper seat. If any of these arguments seems persuasive to you, transfer your wonder to the wisdom of God who arranged things this way. For amazement at the greatest things is not diminished when the manner in which something marvelous happens is discovered. But if not, then at least let the simplicity of faith be stronger than logical demonstrations.

We might say the same things about heaven as well: the wise men of the world have composed very many-worded treatises about the heavenly nature. Some have said that it is composed of the four elements, since it is tangible and visible, sharing in earth because of its resistance, in fire because it is seen, and in the remaining elements because of the mixture. Others, rejecting this argument as unconvincing, introduced a certain fifth nature of body for the constitution of heaven, improvising it from themselves and by themselves. And among them there is something called the ethereal body, which they say is neither fire nor air nor earth nor water, nor in general any one of the simple bodies. They reason that the simple bodies have movement in a straight line as their proper motion, light things being carried upward and heavy things downward. But upward and downward are not the same as circular whirling, and in general a straight line differs enormously from revolution in a circle. And things whose natural movements are different must necessarily, they say, also have different essences. But neither can we suppose that heaven is composed of the primary bodies, which we call elements, because things composed of different materials cannot have smooth and unforced movement, since each of the simple bodies present in composite things has one impulse or another from nature. Therefore composite things are first of all held together with labor in their continuous movement, because one movement cannot be well-fitted and congenial to all the opposing elements; rather, the movement proper to the light element is hostile to the heaviest. For when we move upward, we are weighed down by the earthy element; and when we are carried downward, we do violence to the fiery element, dragging it down contrary to nature. And this dragging of the elements in opposite directions is an occasion of falling apart. For what is forced and contrary to nature, after resisting for a little while—and that violently and with difficulty—quickly dissolves into the things from which it was composed, as each of the elements that came together returns to its proper place.

last_rejected.why: συνωσθήσεται means 'will be borne/carried together,' not 'pushed together.' The sense is convergence by natural motion, not compression by external force.
last_rejected.fix: the whole will likewise be borne toward that same place
last_rejected.ruling: συνωσθήσεται can mean 'thrust/pushed together'; natural convergence is captured adequately without misleading the reader.

last_rejected.why: πολυφωνότατοι means 'most noisy' or 'much-babbling,' a pejorative for verbose, pretentious works. 'Many-worded' is too neutral; Basil mocks these treatises.
last_rejected.ruling: πολυφωνότατος here means 'very wordy/verbose'; 'many-worded' conveys this adequately within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: improvising it from themselves and by themselves
last_rejected.why: οἴκοθεν means 'from their own resources/home,' i.e., without evidence; ἀποσχεδιάσαντες means 'extemporizing' or 'making up on the spot.' The English loses the charge of groundless invention.
last_rejected.fix: dreaming it up from their own heads, extemporizing on their own
last_rejected.ruling: 'from themselves and by themselves' captures οἴκοθεν καὶ παρ' ἑαυτῶν; groundless invention is implied adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἄλλην καὶ ἄλλην means 'one and another,' i.e., 'different' impulses, not 'one or another' (vague). The point is conflicting impulses, not variety.
last_rejected.fix: each simple body has a different impulse from nature
last_rejected.ruling: ἄλλην καὶ ἄλλην means 'different'; 'one impulse or another' conveys differing impulses without misleading.

last_rejected.quote: Therefore composite things are first of all held together with labor
last_rejected.source_quote: Διὸ πρῶτον μὲν καμάτῳ συνέχεται ἐν τῇ συνεχεῖ κινήσει τὰ σύνθετα
last_rejected.why: πρῶτον μὲν introduces the first of multiple points, not 'first of all' as emphasis. Better: 'In the first place, composite things are held together with toil in continuous motion.'
last_rejected.fix: In the first place, composite things are held together by toil in their continuous motion
last_rejected.ruling: 'First of all' can introduce first of multiple points; no meaning lost or reader misled.
